source: Indeed ChIP revealed Sgo2-FLAG to be significantly enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-G34V or H3-WT (Figure 5C), and that Sgo2 is highly enriched at ST domains in mst2Δgcn5Δ relative to WT controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Sgo2 normally accumulates at centromeres in mitosis and is recruited to ST in interphase.
source: Since Sgo2 normally accumulates at centromeres in mitosis and is recruited to ST in interphase (Kawashima et al., 2010; Matsuda et al., 2015; Tashiro et al., 2016), we asked whether H3-G34R influences the cell cycle dependence of its localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation.
source: Importantly, Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation (Figure 5E), but even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT (Figure 5F), suggestive that in H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT.
source: Importantly, Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation (Figure 5E), but even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT (Figure 5F), suggestive that in H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: In H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
source: Importantly, Sgo2 accumulation at centromeres in mitosis was unaffected by H3-G34R mutation (Figure 5E), but even in mitotically arrested cells, Sgo2 was preferentially enriched at ST domains in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT (Figure 5F), suggestive that in H3-G34R cells, cell cycle regulation of Sgo2 accumulation at ST is perturbed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Sgo2 accumulates at subtelomeres in H3-G34R or H3K36ac-deficient cells, correlating with enhanced silencing of ST domains and knob formation in these cells.
source: In summary, our data suggest that Sgo2 accumulates at subtelomeres in H3-G34R or H3K36ac-deficient cells, correlating with enhanced silencing of ST domains and knob formation in these cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: H3-G34K cells had elevated Sgo2 at ST sites.
source: We also performed Sgo2 ChIP in H3-G34K cells. Consistent with enhanced Sgo2 recruitment to silenced ST domains seen in H3K36ac acetyltransferase defective and H3-G34R strains, H3-G34K cells also had elevated Sgo2 at ST sites (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: There was no change in H3K36me3 in mixed copy H3-G34R, H3-G34V, or H3-G34K strains compared with 3xH3 WT.
source: We first asked if H3K36me3 was reduced in mixed H3 strains and found no change in H3K36me3 in mixed copy H3-G34R, H3-G34V, or H3-G34K strains compared with 3xH3 WT (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no dominant increase in levels of H3K36me2 when the mutants were expressed in mixed H3 backgrounds.
source: Similarly, we found no dominant increase in levels of H3K36me2 when the mutants were expressed in mixed H3 backgrounds (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: These results are consistent with the lack of dominant effect of G34R or G34V mutations on K36 methylation in mammalian cells.
source: These results are consistent with the lack of dominant effect of G34R or G34V mutations on K36 methylation in mammalian cells (Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of H3K36ac was restricted to the G34R mutant H3 protein in mixed copy H3-G34R strain.
source: We found that loss of H3K36ac was restricted to the G34R mutant H3 protein, whereas K36ac was present at comparable levels on wild-type H3 purified from the mixed copy G34R and wild-type 3xH3 strains (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: K36ac was present at comparable levels on wild-type H3 purified from the mixed copy G34R and wild-type 3xH3 strains.
source: We found that loss of H3K36ac was restricted to the G34R mutant H3 protein, whereas K36ac was present at comparable levels on wild-type H3 purified from the mixed copy G34R and wild-type 3xH3 strains (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Mixed copy strains grew as well as 3xH3 WT strains, with the notable exception of H3-G34R (3xH3), which like the sole copy H3-G34R mutant, grew less well in the presence of HU.
source: Mixed copy strains grew as well as 3xH3 WT strains, with the notable exception of H3-G34R (3xH3), which like the sole copy H3-G34R mutant, grew less well in the presence of HU (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3-G34K and H3-G34V mixed copy strains grew as well as WT (3xH3) strains on bleomycin and zeocin.
source: We also tested sensitivity to IR mimetics, and found that H3-G34K and H3-G34V mixed copy strains grew as well as WT (3xH3) strains on bleomycin and zeocin (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: There was no evidence of increased chromosome loss in the mixed H3 backgrounds for either H3-G34K or H3-G34R.
source: In contrast to the chromosome missegregation seen in H3-G34R and H3-G34K sole copy strains, there was no evidence of increased chromosome loss in the mixed H3 backgrounds for either H3-G34K or H3-G34R (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: There was a significant drop in efficiency for H3-G34R mixed copy strains in the plasmid-based HR DNA repair assay.
source: There was however a significant drop in efficiency for H3-G34R mixed copy strains in our plasmid-based HR DNA repair assay (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: The overall numbers of genes that are differentially expressed in the (3xH3) background are reduced compared with the number of differentially regulated genes in the sole copy strains.
source: We note that the overall numbers of genes that are differentially expressed in the (3xH3) background are reduced compared with the number of differentially regulated genes in the sole copy strains (54 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34R (3xH3) vs 160 genes in H3-G34R, and 142 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34K (3xH3) vs 223 in H3-G34K when using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), suggestive that the presence of wild-type H3 partially overrides some transcriptional effects of the mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The presence of wild-type H3 partially overrides some transcriptional effects of the mutants.
source: We note that the overall numbers of genes that are differentially expressed in the (3xH3) background are reduced compared with the number of differentially regulated genes in the sole copy strains (54 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34R (3xH3) vs 160 genes in H3-G34R, and 142 genes differentially expressed in H3-G34K (3xH3) vs 223 in H3-G34K when using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), suggestive that the presence of wild-type H3 partially overrides some transcriptional effects of the mutants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The majority of genes influenced by mutation in the (3xH3) background were also differentially regulated in the sole copy backgrounds.
source: Using the more relaxed criteria of p<0.05, we found that the majority of genes influenced by mutation in the (3xH3) background were also differentially regulated in the sole copy backgrounds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Subtelomeric domains of chromosomes I and II were repressed in H3-G34R mixed copy strains compared with WT H3 (3xH3).
source: Manhattan plots indicated that subtelomeric domains of chromosomes I and II were repressed in H3-G34R mixed copy strains compared with WT H3 (3xH3), with a similar, but less marked trend also in H3-G34K mixed copy strains (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: A similar, but less marked trend of ST domain repression was also seen in H3-G34K mixed copy strains.
source: Manhattan plots indicated that subtelomeric domains of chromosomes I and II were repressed in H3-G34R mixed copy strains compared with WT H3 (3xH3), with a similar, but less marked trend also in H3-G34K mixed copy strains (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: A high proportion of genes repressed in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident within ST domains (10/30 and 25/69, respectively).
source: Extending this analysis to ask if subtelomeric domains were preferentially repressed in H3-G34R or H3-G34K mixed copy strains (using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), we found that a high proportion of genes repressed in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident with ST domains (10/30 and 25/69, respectively) compared with only 1/24 and 7/73 of genes activated in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains (Supplemental Table S4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Only 1/24 and 7/73 of genes activated in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident within ST domains.
source: Extending this analysis to ask if subtelomeric domains were preferentially repressed in H3-G34R or H3-G34K mixed copy strains (using FDR 5% and FC of 1.5), we found that a high proportion of genes repressed in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains were resident with ST domains (10/30 and 25/69, respectively) compared with only 1/24 and 7/73 of genes activated in G34R and G34K mixed copy strains (Supplemental Table S4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Many of the genes that are repressed by the H3-G34R or G34K mutation are situated in ST domains of chromosomes I and II.
source: Thus many of the genes that are repressed by the H3-G34R or G34K mutation are situated in ST domains of chromosomes I and II, and the hyper-repression of gene expression within ST domains is dominant since it is evident in the mixed copy background strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The hyper-repression of gene expression within ST domains is dominant since it is evident in the mixed copy background strains.
source: Thus many of the genes that are repressed by the H3-G34R or G34K mutation are situated in ST domains of chromosomes I and II, and the hyper-repression of gene expression within ST domains is dominant since it is evident in the mixed copy background strains.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data comparing sole copy and mixed copy strains.

claim: Activity of the H3K36 tri-methylase SETD2 is blocked on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations.
source: However, consistent with a defect in tri-methylation, a very recent report shows that activity of the H3K36 tri-methylase SETD2 is blocked on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations, whereas NSD2-mediated di-methylation is unaffected (Jain et al., 2020), although in that study, G34R, G34V, and G34W similarly affected tri-methylation, whereas we saw no defect in H3K36me3 in the H3-G34W mutant, or H3-G34M, or G34Q strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NSD2-mediated di-methylation is unaffected on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations.
source: However, consistent with a defect in tri-methylation, a very recent report shows that activity of the H3K36 tri-methylase SETD2 is blocked on nucleosomes bearing H3.3 G34 mutations, whereas NSD2-mediated di-methylation is unaffected (Jain et al., 2020), although in that study, G34R, G34V, and G34W similarly affected tri-methylation, whereas we saw no defect in H3K36me3 in the H3-G34W mutant, or H3-G34M, or G34Q strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Fission yeast H3 differs from H3.3 at several residues including alanines instead of serines at residues 28 and 31 within the H3 tail.
source: Another possibility is that the differences in K36me3 stem from our analysis of fission yeast H3, which differs from H3.3 at several residues including alanines instead of serines at residues 28 and 31 within the H3 tail (Matsumoto and Yanagida, 1985; Yadav et al., 2017), which may influence K36 methyltransferase behavior on G34 mutant templates (Schuhmacher et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Co-expression of mutant (H3-G34R, V, or K) with wild-type H3 proteins did not affect H3K36me3.
source: However, consistent with previous studies in mammalian cells, we found that co-expression of mutant (H3-G34R, V, or K) with wild-type H3 proteins did not affect H3K36me3, suggesting that if indeed Set2 activity is altered, loss of Set2-mediated trimethylation of K36 is limited to the mutant H3 tail.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: If Set2 activity is altered, loss of Set2-mediated trimethylation of K36 is limited to the mutant H3 tail.
source: However, consistent with previous studies in mammalian cells, we found that co-expression of mutant (H3-G34R, V, or K) with wild-type H3 proteins did not affect H3K36me3, suggesting that if indeed Set2 activity is altered, loss of Set2-mediated trimethylation of K36 is limited to the mutant H3 tail.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: In fission yeast, H3-G34R mutants with reduced K36ac and K36me3 are defective for HR-mediated repair of DNA breaks.
source: K36 modifications have been linked to DNA damage response. In fission yeast, H3-G34R mutants with reduced K36ac and K36me3 are defective for HR-mediated repair of DNA breaks, whilst H3-G34V mutants, which maintain K36ac but have reduced K36me3, show no defect in HR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H3-G34V mutants, which maintain K36ac but have reduced K36me3, show no defect in HR.
source: K36 modifications have been linked to DNA damage response. In fission yeast, H3-G34R mutants with reduced K36ac and K36me3 are defective for HR-mediated repair of DNA breaks, whilst H3-G34V mutants, which maintain K36ac but have reduced K36me3, show no defect in HR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduction in K36me3 is not causal of the HR defect.
source: Since both mutants (and HR-proficient H3-G34K) have reduced H3K36me3, reduction in K36me3 is not causal of the HR defect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claim: Gcn5 mutants are reduced for H3K36ac, are HU sensitive, and are also defective for HR.
source: However, like H3-G34R mutants, Gcn5 mutants are reduced for H3K36ac, are HU sensitive, and are also defective for HR (Pai et al., 2014); so these phenotypes may be linked.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast.
source: We confirmed that Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast and then showed in vitro that Gcn5 activity was lost specifically at K36 on recombinant G34R H3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Gcn5 activity was lost specifically at K36 on recombinant G34R H3 in vitro.
source: We confirmed that Gcn5 is the major H3K36 acetyltransferase in fission yeast and then showed in vitro that Gcn5 activity was lost specifically at K36 on recombinant G34R H3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: H3-G34R directly affects Gcn5 function.
source: This result emphasizes that H3-G34R directly affects Gcn5 function, but meant that we could not bypass the K36 acetylation defect in H3-G34R cells by Gcn5 overexpression to assign specific phenotypes to loss of H3K36ac.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing loss of Gcn5 activity on G34R H3.

claim: It remains unclear whether the HR defect and sensitivity to HU seen in G34R cells are caused by loss of H3K36ac.
source: It therefore remains unclear whether the HR defect and sensitivity to HU seen in G34R cells are caused by loss of H3K36ac.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the limitation of the current data in establishing causality.

claim: The histone mutants disrupt the local chromatin architecture such that deposition of H3-G34R at leu1 reduces local levels of K36ac and disrupts HR at that locus.
source: However, since chromatin is assembled from nucleosomes bearing two copies of H3, one possibility is that even in the presence of excess WT H3, H3K36ac is sufficiently diluted to cause dominant defects in HR and dominant HU sensitivity. In other words, the histone mutants disrupt the local chromatin architecture such that deposition of H3-G34R at leu1 reduces local levels of K36ac and disrupts HR at that locus.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Similar explanations have been suggested for local dominant roles of other histone mutants identified in cancer.
source: Similar explanations have been suggested for local dominant roles of other histone mutants identified in cancer (Nacev et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The unique phenotypes of H3-G34R mutants may be due to the generation of a novel site of arginine methylation within the H3 tail.
source: Another possibility would be that the unique phenotypes of H3-G34R mutants are due to the generation of a novel site of arginine methylation within the H3 tail. We have used mass spectroscopy to explore this possibility, but found no evidence for methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast (Lowe et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculative but tested experimentally, with no evidence found for arginine methylation.

claim: No evidence was found for methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast.
source: Another possibility would be that the unique phenotypes of H3-G34R mutants are due to the generation of a novel site of arginine methylation within the H3 tail. We have used mass spectroscopy to explore this possibility, but found no evidence for methylation of H3-G34R in fission yeast (Lowe et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to published work.

claim: Local perturbation of chromatin structure from deposition of the mutant histones is insufficient to yield IR sensitivity in the presence of wild-type H3.
source: In contrast to H3-G34R cells, which are not sensitive to γ-IR, both H3-G34V and H3-G34K are sensitive to γ-IR and to IR-mimetics but there was no dominant effect since mixed copy strains were not sensitive to IR mimetics. This may mean that local perturbation of chromatin structure from deposition of the mutant histones is insufficient to yield IR sensitivity in the presence of wild-type H3.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing sole copy and mixed copy strains.

claim: Substitution of G34 with basic residues K or R led to accumulation of Sgo2 at subtelomeric (ST) domains correlating with enhanced silencing of these regions.
source: We also found that substitution of G34 with basic residues K or R led to accumulation of Sgo2 at subtelomeric (ST) domains correlating with enhanced silencing of these regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Cells defective for gcn5Δ and mst2Δ show repression of ST domains.
source: Cells defective for gcn5Δ and mst2Δ similarly show repression of ST domains (Nugent et al., 2010), and we found that they accumulate Sgo2 at ST domains and, like G34R, accumulate knobs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: At ST domains, Sgo2 controls the timing of replication of late replicating origins.
source: At ST domains, Sgo2 controls the timing of replication of late replicating origins, and loss of Sgo2 advances replication of some ST origins (Tashiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of Sgo2 advances replication of some ST origins.
source: At ST domains, Sgo2 controls the timing of replication of late replicating origins, and loss of Sgo2 advances replication of some ST origins (Tashiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The elevated levels of Sgo2 at ST domains in H3-G34R, H3-G34K, and H3K36 acetyltransferase mutants may further delay the timing of late-replicating ST origins, leading to chromosome mis-segregation, as well as replicative stress sensitivity.
source: One possibility is that the elevated levels of Sgo2 at ST domains in H3-G34R, H3-G34K, and H3K36 acetyltransferase mutants further delays the timing of late-replicating ST origins, leading to chromosome mis-segregation, as well as replicative stress sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data and published literature.

claim: The aberrant accumulation of Sgo2 at ST domains in mitotic H3-G34R cells could indirectly perturb centromere function.
source: Alternately, the aberrant accumulation of Sgo2 at ST domains in mitotic H3-G34R cells could indirectly perturb centromere function. This is not due to depletion of Sgo2 from centromeres (as centromeric Sgo2 accumulation is similar between G34R and wild-type cells), but perhaps from mislocalization and/or depletion of a limiting factor that is normally recruited by Sgo2 to centromeres in mitosis, and that in G34R cells is now retargeted preferentially to ST domains.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Silencing of ST domains is maintained in mixed copy strains, whereas chromosome missegregation is corrected.
source: However, we note that silencing of ST domains is maintained in mixed copy strains, whereas chromosome missegregation is corrected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Recruitment of Shugoshin proteins relies on Bub1 kinase-mediated phosphorylation of histone H2A on S121 (T120 in mammals).
source: What is clear from many organisms is that recruitment of Shugoshin proteins relies on Bub1 kinase-mediated phosphorylation of histone H2A on S121 (T120 in mammals) (Kawashima et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2005; Kitajima et al., 2004; Matsuda et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2004; Tashiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both Bub1 kinase dead and H2A-S121A mutants lose localization of Sgo2 from centromeres and subtelomeres in fission yeast.
source: In fission yeast, both Bub1 kinase dead and H2A-S121A mutants lose localization of Sgo2 from centromeres and subtelomeres (Tashiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: H3-G34R mutants alter the kinetics of phosphorylation at residues S128/129 of histone H2A.
source: We previously reported that H3-G34R mutants also alter the kinetics of phosphorylation at residues S128/129 of histone H2A (Yadav et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The G34R and G34K mutant H3s may influence signaling through multiple phosphorylation sites clustered on the C-terminus of H2A.
source: Together with our new finding that H3-G34R/K mutants influence the localization of Sgo2, these data suggest the possibility that the G34R and G34K mutant H3s influence signaling through multiple phosphorylation sites clustered on the C-terminus of H2A.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The C-terminus of H2A lies close to the site of G34 substitutions on the H3 N-terminal tail.
source: This is consistent with structural analyses of nucleosomes showing that the C-terminus of H2A lies close to the site of G34 substitutions on the H3 N-terminal tail (Du and Briggs, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The homolog of Sgo2, SGO1 in budding yeast has been shown to bind histone H3.
source: We note that an interesting functional link between H3 and Shugoshin has also been made in budding yeast, where the homolog of Sgo2, SGO1 has been shown to bind histone H3.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about budding yeast.

claim: SGO1 binds a 'tension-sensing motif' at residues 42–45 on H3, which is necessary for Sgo1 recruitment to centromeres and for efficient chromosome segregation during mitosis.
source: Although not reliant on G34 or K36 residues of H3, SGO1 binds a 'tension-sensing motif' at residues 42–45 on H3, which is necessary for Sgo1 recruitment to centromeres and for efficient chromosome segregation during mitosis (Deng and Kuo, 2018; Luo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 is important for ensuring efficient chromosome segregation when the tension sensing motif is damaged in budding yeast.
source: Intriguingly in this system, the histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 is important for ensuring efficient chromosome segregation when the tension sensing motif is damaged (Buehl et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: H3.3G34 mutants in mammalian cells exert profound transcriptional effects through modulation of Polycomb activity.
source: In keeping with the importance of transcriptional regulation in H3-G34 mutant cells, very recent work from the Lewis lab indicates that H3.3G34 mutants in mammalian cells exert profound transcriptional effects through modulation of Polycomb activity (Jain et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The decrease in K36me3 on H3.3 G34 mutant histone enhances PRC2 activity to promote elevated H3.3K27me3 in cis on the H3.3 tail.
source: They found that the decrease in K36me3 on H3.3 G34 mutant histone enhances PRC2 activity to promote elevated H3.3K27me3 in cis on the H3.3 tail (Jain et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tumorigenesis driven by H3.3G34 mutations derives from enhanced Polycomb-mediated silencing of enhancers of genes that regulate differentiation, whereby cells retain a more stem cell-like fate.
source: They propose that tumorigenesis driven by H3.3G34 mutations derives from enhanced Polycomb-mediated silencing of enhancers of genes that regulate differentiation, whereby cells retain a more stem cell-like fate.
evidence: This claim is based on a proposal from published literature.

claim: Acetylation at enhancers principally resides on K27 of histone H3.3.
source: Since acetylation at enhancers principally resides on K27 of histone H3.3 (Martire et al., 2019), this may explain why the G34 mutations identified in cancer occur solely on H3.3 (Behjati et al., 2013; Schwartzentruber et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The G34 mutations identified in cancer occur solely on H3.3.
source: Since acetylation at enhancers principally resides on K27 of histone H3.3 (Martire et al., 2019), this may explain why the G34 mutations identified in cancer occur solely on H3.3 (Behjati et al., 2013; Schwartzentruber et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: H3.3 only differs from H3.2 by four residues: Ser31 in the tail, and three substitutions within the core of H3 which dictate chaperone selectivity.
source: H3.3 only differs from H3.2 by four residues: Ser31 in the tail, and three substitutions within the core of H3 which dictate chaperone selectivity (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002; Elsässer et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser31 in H3.3 is important for regulation of cell fate during gastrulation and for enhancer activation.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser31 in H3.3 is important for regulation of cell fate during gastrulation and for enhancer activation (Martire et al., 2019; Sitbon et al., 2020) and Ser31P influences H3.3 K27 trimethylation and acetylation (Martire et al., 2019; Sitbon et al., 2020), and so phosphoregulation via S31 may provide an additional mechanistic link as to why the Gly 34 mutations are only found in H3.3.

claim: Ser31P influences H3.3 K27 trimethylation and acetylation.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser31 in H3.3 is important for regulation of cell fate during gastrulation and for enhancer activation (Martire et al., 2019; Sitbon et al., 2020) and Ser31P influences H3.3 K27 trimethylation and acetylation (Martire et al., 2019; Sitbon et al., 2020), and so phosphoregulation via S31 may provide an additional mechanistic link as to why the Gly 34 mutations are only found in H3.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from published literature.

claim: Fission yeast lacks a Polycomb silencing pathway.
source: Although fission yeast provides an exquisite system for analysis of histone mutations, we fully acknowledge the limitation of work in a system that lacks a Polycomb silencing pathway.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about fission yeast.
